analysis: Reviewed the two head_text excerpts of fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json (lines 33272-34875) along with the patch excerpt and change ranges. This is a test-fixture JSON file containing prompt-contract golden vectors: request/provider/template inputs, token IDs, plan hashes and block boundaries. The visible excerpts contain only literal synthetic content ("fixture-scope" scope IDs, fake dates, repeated filler tokens, tool schemas like weather/forecast). I found no secrets, keys, credentials, endpoints or executable code. The patch excerpt shows additional_context {enable_thinking:false} added to a template input, with prompt_token_count and chain_hash values regenerated and a block boundary removed. That is a prompt-rendering contract change in test vectors, not an authorization, attestation, encryption or billing control. Relevant threat context is the prefix cache in T-041 (oversized, not fully visible) and the consumer/provider prompt boundary in TB-002/A-001. Chain hashes and prompt_contract_id values bind cache keys to rendered prompts, so a divergence between the fixtures and the runtime implementation could affect cache-key correctness. The supplied evidence does not show the implementing source (Swift or Go prompt planner), so I cannot verify that the new contract preserves scope isolation (scope_id) or that the cache-boundary semantics are unchanged. In the visible fragments, scope_id remains "fixture-scope" across vectors, so no isolation regression is evident. Open question for integration: check that the code changes accompanying these regenerated vectors (the enable_thinking additional_context and the token-count and boundary changes) do not weaken scope binding of prefix-cache chain hashes. Nothing in these units establishes a concrete security regression. The patch excerpt is truncated and the file's other changed ranges (for example 3805, 43739, 52354) were not visible in the supplied units.
